summary: Describes the guidelines and procedures for forming and running IETF working groups. It covers how groups are chartered, how chairs work, how consensus is reached and how groups close. It is a Best Current Practice and has since been updated by several later documents.

eli5.summary: This is the rule book for how teams of volunteers inside the IETF form, hold meetings and make decisions together.

subtitle: The rulebook for how IETF working groups are formed, run, staffed and closed down.

tldr.problem: The IETF does its standards work in working groups, and those groups need shared rules for how they start, how they decide things, who does what, and when they stop.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2418 sets out a chartering process approved by the IESG, decision-making by rough consensus, open meetings and mailing lists, defined staff roles such as the Chair, and a path from Internet-Draft to RFC.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 25) that obsoletes RFC 1603. Later RFCs, namely 3934, 7475, 7776, 8717, 9141 and 9945, update it, so read it together with them.

sections.title: Where Working Groups Fit
sections.content:
The IETF is a large, open community of network designers, operators, vendors, users and researchers. Its main work is done by committees called working groups (WGs). Each has a narrow focus and a lifetime bounded by a specific set of tasks, although there are exceptions. At the time of writing the RFC counts more than 100 working groups.

For management, working groups are gathered into areas, each managed by one or two Area Directors (ADs). The Area Directors, together with the IETF Chair, make up the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG), which approves IETF standards and the publication of other IETF documents.

There is no formal membership in the IETF. Participation is open to all, and people take part as individual technical contributors rather than as representatives of organizations.
sections.eli5: The IETF is like a huge club with lots of small project teams. Anyone can join in, and each team works on one job at a time.

sections.title: Forming a Working Group
sections.content:
A working group may start at the initiative of an Area Director or of an individual or group. Anyone who wants to create one MUST obtain the advice and consent of the Area Director(s) for the relevant area and follow the formal steps. Groups are expected to be short-lived: they are created for a specific problem or deliverable and are terminated when it is done.

Before agreeing, the Area Director and the IESG weigh criteria such as these:

  • Are the issues clear and relevant, and are the goals specific and achievable in a reasonable time?
  • Does the work overlap with another working group or another standards body?
  • Is there enough interest and expertise? The RFC says experience suggests a minimum of four or five active people in management positions, plus one or two dozen who attend meetings and contribute on the mailing list.
  • Is the effort broader than the activity of a single vendor, and does the IETF have a real role in shaping the technology?

An Area Director may also require a Birds of a Feather (BOF) session first. A BOF is a session at an IETF meeting for exploration and brainstorming. It needs Area Director approval, a description and agenda, and a report from its Chair. A BOF on a topic normally meets once, may meet a second time in unusual circumstances, and is not permitted to meet three times.
sections.eli5: Before a new team can start, grown-ups check that the job is clear, enough people care, and nobody else is already doing it. Sometimes they hold a trial meeting first to see if people are interested.

sections.title: The Charter
sections.content:
Every working group needs a charter, which the RFC calls a contract between the working group and the IETF to perform a set of tasks. It is negotiated mainly between a prospective Chair and the Area Director(s), and finally approved by the IESG with advice from the Internet Architecture Board (IAB).

A charter contains:

  • A name and an acronym of at most 8 printable ASCII characters.
  • The Chair(s), generally limited to two, plus the area, the Area Director(s) and the responsible Area Director.
  • A mailing list, with subscription details and a public archive. The list MUST be copied to the Secretariat archive address.
  • A description of the group's focus, covering architecture, operations, security, network management, scaling and transition where applicable.
  • Goals and milestones with dates. Milestones must be real deliverables: "Internet-Draft finished" is fine, but "discuss via email" is not. Milestones every 3 to 6 months are suggested.

After Area Director approval, the charter goes to the IAB for review and the IESG for approval. After a review period of at least a week it is posted to the IETF-announce and new-work mailing lists, and after another review period of at least a week the IESG may approve it, request changes or decline. The Appendix gives a sample charter for an IP Telephony group.
sections.eli5: A charter is the team's promise: what it will build, who is in charge, where people can talk, and when each piece will be done.

sections.title: How a Working Group Operates
sections.content:
Within the IETF's requirements for open and fair participation and thorough consideration of alternatives, each working group is autonomous. The core rule is rough consensus. It does not require everyone to agree, but the dominant view prevails, and "dominance" is not decided by volume or persistence. The RFC notes that 51% of a group does not qualify as rough consensus and 99% is better than rough. The Chair decides whether rough consensus has been reached.

Other operating rules include:

  • All working group actions are taken in a public forum. The Chair MUST publish a draft agenda well in advance, and documents to be discussed should be available as Internet-Drafts at least two weeks before a session.
  • Every session, including interim ones, is reported with minutes: the agenda, an account of the discussion and decisions, and an attendee list.
  • Email permits the widest participation. Decisions made face to face on topics not discussed on the list, or that differ significantly from list consensus, MUST be reviewed on the mailing list.
  • To keep progress moving, a Chair may reject or defer input that is old, minor, badly timed or out of scope.
  • For disruptive behavior, the Chair first communicates with the individual directly, then involves the Area Director. As a last resort the Area Director, with IESG approval, may ask that the person's ability to post be blocked, though not their ability to receive messages.

Disputes are resolved by open review and discussion, using the procedures in RFC 2026 for review of WG, Chair, Area Director or IESG actions.
sections.eli5: The team does not need everybody to agree on everything, but it must be a real, broad agreement and not just the loudest voices. Everything is done in the open and written down in meeting notes.

sections.title: Staff Roles and Closing a Group
sections.content:
The WG Chair has wide discretion and is responsible for forward progress through a fair and open process. Duties include moderating the mailing list, planning and running sessions, making sure minutes are taken, sending the Area Director a short report right after each session, spreading the workload and seeing that authors incorporate agreed changes. The Chair and the Document Editor are generally different people.

Other roles are:

  • Secretary: records decisions and edits documents rather than performing basic specification.
  • Document Editor: ensures a document accurately reflects the group's decisions.
  • Facilitator: handles process management when meetings become distracted or divisive.
  • Design team: a small sub-group that may have closed membership, whose output is always subject to approval by the whole WG.
  • Consultant: a senior participant the Area Director may assign.
  • Area Director: responsible for coherent, coordinated and timely output in the area.

Groups normally disband when their tasks are complete, though a group that produced a Proposed or Draft Standard often becomes dormant, keeping its mailing list open. If a group cannot finish its charter, the Area Director, in consultation with the group, can recharter it, choose new Chair(s) or disband it. Rechartering follows the same procedure as the original chartering, and the group may appeal to the IESG if it disagrees.
sections.eli5: A team has a captain who keeps things fair and moving, a note taker, an editor who writes down what was agreed, and sometimes a referee for heated moments. When the job is done, the team stops.

sections.title: From Draft to RFC
sections.content:
Working documents live as Internet-Drafts, which the RFC stresses have no official standards status whatsoever. They may become standards-track documents or sink from sight. An Internet-Draft must contain the standard boilerplate, its filename and an expiration date.

When a group decides a document is ready, the Chair usually issues a working group Last-Call. After at least rough consensus exists, the exact version agreed MUST be in the Internet-Drafts directory, formatted as an RFC, and the Chair MUST email the Area Director with a copy to the IESG Secretariat. The IESG then takes responsibility unless it returns the document.

The IESG reviews every document submitted for publication. For standards-track documents the Secretariat issues an IETF Last-Call lasting two weeks, meant as a brief final check rather than an in-depth review. The IESG can accept the document as is, accept it for a different status, suggest changes, or reject it with specific arguments. The RFC series is a publication mechanism only: all Internet Standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.
sections.eli5: Ideas start as rough drafts that anyone can read. When the team agrees one is ready, a senior group checks it one more time before it is published for good.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says documents describing IETF processes do not affect the security of network infrastructure or Internet applications. It does remind readers that every working group is required to examine and understand the security implications of the technology it develops. That analysis must appear in a Security Considerations section of the resulting RFCs, and merely noting a significant security hole is no longer sufficient.
sections.eli5: Every team must check whether what it builds could be unsafe, and write down how it handles that.
